narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 71.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile is far below the average ranking of accepted students, signaling that your later-year performance was unusually weak compared with those who succeeded. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; again, a bottom-decile placement is much lower than the typical accepted student.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 2.70 it is below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, yet the model still saw this value as a modest positive signal that slightly increased the chance you might pass. Unfortunately, this encouraging nudge was not nearly large enough to offset the negative impact of your two class-rank indicators.

Your LSAT score of 29, middle-family income, and plan to attend full-time were less influential in the final decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in any remaining coursework, consider retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s, and explore structured bar-prep programs that have helped students with similar profiles succeed on a second attempt.
